frcgw-01.name: Your Withholding Position
frcgw-01.desc: Whether withholding applies to your sale, and how the 15% is worked out.
frcgw-01.content:
Your withholding position

The three facts

1. From 1 January 2025 there is no value threshold — every Australian real property sale is in scope, whatever the price.

2. If a valid clearance certificate is not given to the purchaser at or before settlement, the purchaser must withhold 15% of the sale price and remit it to the ATO.

3. A clearance certificate is free, most issue within days, and it stays valid for 12 months. There is no obligation to use one you obtain.

How the amount is worked out

Withholding = sale price x 15%. It is calculated on the sale price, not on your profit, and not on the capital gain. That is why it can exceed the tax you actually owe — and why it is credited back to you rather than kept.

Your sale price: {{bind:sale_price|this check did not ask for your sale price, so we have not put a figure here. Multiply your contract price by 0.15 to get the amount that would be withheld.}}

Worked examples

These are illustrations, not your numbers.

Sale price (example)Withheld at 15% (example)
$450,000$67,500
$900,000$135,000
$1,200,000$180,000

In each case the amount is remitted to the ATO and credited to the vendor when they lodge the return for the income year the contract was signed.

{{#if section:per_vendor}}

You co-own this property — the 15% is per owner

A clearance certificate covers one vendor, not one property. Each owner named on the title applies separately and the applications are processed separately, so they can issue on different days.

If one co-owner's certificate is missing at settlement, the purchaser withholds 15% of that owner's share of the sale price. The other owners are unaffected. On a $600,000 sale held equally by two owners, one missing certificate means 15% of $300,000 — $45,000 — is withheld for that owner alone. Again, an illustration, not your figures.

Each certificate is free, so there is nothing to gain by waiting until every owner is ready to apply together.

{{/if}}{{#unless state:settled}}{{#if has:settlement_date}}

Your dates

Settlement: {{bind:settlement_date}}

Lodge by: {{bind:lodge_by_date}} — 28 days out, which is the outer processing time the ATO asks you to allow. Most certificates issue well inside that.

{{/if}}{{#unless has:settlement_date}}

Your dates

You did not give us a settlement date, so this pack does not state one. Put your settlement date in your calendar and count back 28 days — that is the date to lodge by if you want the full margin the ATO asks you to allow.

{{/unless}}{{/unless}}{{#if state:settled}}

Your dates

Your settlement has already happened, so there is no lodge-by date left to work towards on this sale. The date that matters now is the end of the income year in which the contract was signed — that is the return the withheld amount is claimed in.

{{/if}}

Source: ATO — Foreign resident capital gains withholding · TAA 1953 Sch 1 Subdiv 14-D

frcgw-02.name: Applying For Your Clearance Certificate
frcgw-02.desc: Who applies, what the form asks, and when to lodge.
frcgw-02.content:
Applying for your clearance certificate

{{#if state:pending}}

You have already lodged. This file is here for reference — there is nothing further for you to apply for. Go to File 03 for what to send the purchaser's side while your application is pending.

{{/if}}{{#if section:recovery}}

You did not hold a certificate at settlement — there is nothing to apply for on this sale; File 07 is your route. This file is here for reference, and for the next property you sell. A certificate obtained now cannot change what was withheld at a settlement that has already happened.

{{/if}}{{#if state:have_cert}}

You already hold a certificate and provided it. There is nothing further to apply for on this sale. This file is here for reference — a certificate stays valid for 12 months, so it may still cover another sale in that window.

{{/if}}

Step 1 — Confirm which instrument you need

{{#if section:variation}}

You have told us you are not an Australian resident for tax purposes. A clearance certificate is not available to you. The instrument for a foreign resident is a variation notice — see File 08, which is the one to read first.

{{/if}}{{#unless section:variation}}

Australian residents for tax purposes apply for a clearance certificate. It is free, and it tells the purchaser they do not need to withhold.

Foreign residents cannot get a clearance certificate. They apply for a variation notice instead, which can set the withholding rate anywhere between 0% and 14.99% where there are real grounds.

{{/unless}}{{#if section:residency_first}}

Your residency is unconfirmed, so start here. Tax residency is not citizenship, not visa status and not Medicare eligibility — it turns on where you actually live and the ties you keep to Australia. The ATO's online residency tests will give you a defensible answer in a few minutes, and the answer decides which of the two applications above you lodge.

{{/if}}

Step 2 — Have the details ready

The application is a short online form. It asks for identity and property details, not a document bundle. File 04 lists exactly what it asks for.

Step 3 — Lodge it

Apply online at ato.gov.au/clearancecertificate. There is no fee. You do not need a tax agent to do it, though your conveyancer or accountant can lodge on your behalf.

Step 4 — When to lodge

Most clearance certificates issue within days. The ATO asks sellers to allow up to 28, because some applications are checked manually.

The certificate is free, valid for 12 months, and you are under no obligation to use it. So the sensible time to apply is as soon as you are thinking of selling — before you list, not once a contract is signed. Applying early takes settlement timing out of the picture entirely.

{{#if section:validity_12_months}}

The 12-month validity window

A certificate is valid for 12 months from the date it is issued, provided your residency status does not change in that period. What the purchaser needs is a certificate that is valid on the settlement date.

{{/if}}{{#if section:reapplication}}

Your contract runs longer than 12 months. A certificate obtained when the contract was signed can expire before settlement. Time the application against your settlement date rather than the contract date — and if the first one lapses, apply again. A fresh certificate is free.

{{/if}}

Step 5 — Give it to the purchaser's side

Once issued, the certificate goes from you (or your conveyancer or solicitor, acting for you as vendor) to the purchaser or their representative — that is who has the withholding obligation and who needs to hold it. Confirm receipt in writing. File 03 has the wording.

{{#unless state:settled}}{{#if has:settlement_date}}

Your settlement: {{bind:settlement_date}}. Lodge by: {{bind:lodge_by_date}} to allow the full 28 days.

{{/if}}{{/unless}}

frcgw-03.name: What To Send The Purchaser's Side
frcgw-03.desc: Wording for handing over the certificate, or for putting them on notice that one is pending.
frcgw-03.content:
What to send the purchaser's side

The purchaser (or their conveyancer or solicitor) carries the withholding obligation. Clear written communication is what stops a default-to-withholding decision being made on the day without anyone asking you.

{{#if section:pending_notice}}

Your certificate is pending — put them on notice now

Pending-notice template

To: [purchaser's conveyancer or solicitor]

Re: Settlement of [property address]{{#if has:settlement_date}}, scheduled {{bind:settlement_date}}{{/if}}

Subject: Foreign resident capital gains withholding — clearance certificate pending

We act for / I am the vendor in the above matter. An application for an ATO clearance certificate under TAA 1953 Schedule 1 Subdivision 14-D has been lodged and is currently pending.

We will forward the certificate as soon as it issues. Please confirm receipt of this notice, and please contact us before settlement if the certificate has not reached you, so that the position can be dealt with rather than defaulted.

[Your name / your conveyancer]

This does not remove the purchaser's obligation — if no certificate is held at settlement they must still withhold. What it does is make sure the position is known in advance rather than discovered on the day.

{{/if}}{{#if section:recovery}}

There is nothing to send about the withholding

Your settlement has completed and an amount was withheld, so the transaction is finished. There is no certificate to transmit and no instruction that would change what happened on the day — the templates below would only apply to a settlement still ahead of you.

What to request instead

To: [purchaser's conveyancer or solicitor]

Re: Settlement of [property address]

Subject: Foreign resident capital gains withholding — payment confirmation

An amount was withheld from the vendor's proceeds at settlement and remitted to the ATO under TAA 1953 Schedule 1 Subdivision 14-D. Please provide a copy of the purchaser's payment notification to the ATO, together with confirmation of the amount remitted and the date of payment.

[Your name / your conveyancer]

Keep that confirmation with your settlement papers. It is the document that evidences the credit when the return for the income year the contract was signed is prepared — see File 07.

{{/if}}{{#unless section:recovery}}{{#unless section:pending_notice}}

Handing over the certificate

Cover-note template

To: [purchaser's conveyancer or solicitor]

Re: Settlement of [property address]{{#if has:settlement_date}}, scheduled {{bind:settlement_date}}{{/if}}

Subject: ATO clearance certificate — foreign resident capital gains withholding

Please find attached the ATO clearance certificate for the vendor in the above matter, issued under TAA 1953 Schedule 1 Subdivision 14-D. The vendor name on the certificate matches the vendor name on the title.

On the basis of this certificate no amount is required to be withheld at settlement. Please confirm receipt by return email.

[Your name / your conveyancer]

{{/unless}}{{/unless}}{{#if section:name_match}}

Check the name before you send it

The most common reason a certificate is queried at settlement is a name mismatch. The name on the certificate must match the vendor name on the title exactly.

Things that catch people out: a middle name present on one and not the other; a maiden or former name on the title; a trustee selling in a trustee capacity; a company name with or without "Pty Ltd"; a deceased estate where the title is in the deceased's name.

Check it now, against the title, not on settlement morning. If it does not match, apply again with the name as it appears on the title — a fresh certificate is free.

{{/if}}{{#if section:keep_a_copy}}

Keep your own copy

Keep the certificate and the confirmation of receipt with your settlement papers. If the withholding is ever queried later, that pair of documents is the answer.

{{/if}}

Confirm, do not assume

Ask for a written acknowledgement. "Sent" is not "received", and an email that went to a monitored inbox nobody opened is the failure mode this step exists to prevent.

frcgw-04.name: Details To Have Ready
frcgw-04.desc: What the ATO clearance certificate form actually asks you for.
frcgw-04.content:
Details to have ready

The clearance certificate application is a short online form, not a documentary submission. You do not need to assemble an evidence bundle, and the ATO does not ask you to upload tax returns, bank statements or utility bills to get one.

What the form asks for

  • Your full legal name — exactly as it appears on the title. This is the one that matters most; see below.
  • Your tax file number. Providing it is not compulsory, but it lets the ATO match you to your record and is the single biggest factor in the application being processed automatically rather than by hand.
  • Your date of birth, and your Australian business number if you are selling in the course of a business.
  • Contact details — email and phone, so the ATO can reach you if something needs checking.
  • Property details — the address of the property being sold.
  • The residency question. The form asks whether you have lodged an Australian tax return in the last two years, and if not, why not. Have your answer ready; not having lodged is not a bar, it just means the question needs answering.

Why the name has to match the title

The certificate is issued in the name you give. The purchaser's representative checks that name against the vendor name on the title. If the two differ, the certificate may not be accepted and the purchaser may withhold anyway.

Common mismatches: a middle name on one and not the other; a maiden or former name still on the title; selling as trustee; a company name with or without its suffix; a deceased estate.

Check the title first, then complete the form to match it. A second certificate, if you need one, is free.

{{#if section:per_vendor}}

One application per owner

Every owner named on the title lodges their own application, with their own name and their own tax file number. There is no joint application. The applications are processed separately, so they can issue on different days.

{{/if}}{{#if section:residency_first}}

Settle your residency first

The form is built around a residency answer, so it is worth being sure before you lodge. Australian tax residency is not citizenship, not visa status and not Medicare eligibility — it turns on where you actually live and the ties you keep here. The ATO publishes online residency tests that will give you a defensible answer in a few minutes. If they leave you genuinely on the line, that is the point at which an accountant is worth the fee.

{{/if}}{{#if section:variation}}

You are a foreign resident — different form

Everything above describes the clearance certificate, which is not available to you. The variation notice has its own application and asks for the grounds on which you say a lower rate should apply. File 08 covers it.

{{/if}}

Timing

Most applications issue within days. The ATO asks you to allow up to 28 in case yours needs manual checking — most commonly where no tax file number was supplied, or where the residency answer needs a look.

Apply at ato.gov.au/clearancecertificate.

frcgw-05.name: Your Accountant Brief
frcgw-05.desc: The questions worth asking, and the ones you can skip.
frcgw-05.content:
Most sellers do not need an accountant for the clearance certificate itself — the form is short, free, and you can lodge it yourself. These are the questions worth asking if you are already speaking to one, or if one of the situations below applies to you.
{{#if section:residency_first}}

Ask this first

"Am I an Australian resident for tax purposes for this sale?"

Why: it decides which instrument you lodge — a clearance certificate if you are, a variation notice if you are not. You have told us this is unconfirmed, which makes it the only question that needs answering before anything else can be.

{{/if}}

Question 1

"Will I have capital gains tax to pay on this sale, and roughly how much?"

Why: the withholding is 15% of the sale price, while your actual tax is on the gain. Knowing the gap tells you whether the withholding would be a cash-flow issue or roughly what you owe anyway. If the property is your main residence for the whole period you owned it, the answer may be nothing — but you still need the certificate.

Question 2

"Does the name on my title need anything done before I apply?"

Why: trustee capacity, a former name, a deceased estate or a company suffix are the situations where the name on the certificate and the name on the title come apart. An accountant or conveyancer will spot it in a minute; settlement is the wrong place to find out.

Question 3

"Which income year does this sale fall in for my return?"

Why: the capital gains event is the contract date, not the settlement date. That also decides which year's return carries any withholding credit. A contract signed in June and settled in August sits in the earlier income year.

{{#if section:recovery}}

Also ask — an amount was withheld

"An amount was withheld at settlement — when do I get it back and how much?"

Why: the amount was remitted to the ATO and is credited to you in the return for the income year the contract was signed. Your accountant can tell you what that return will look like and roughly when the refund lands. See File 07.

{{/if}}{{#if section:variation}}

Also ask — foreign resident

"Do I have grounds for a variation notice, and at what rate?"

Why: a variation can set the rate between 0% and 14.99%, but only on real grounds — no gain, a reduced liability or losses, or a mortgagee taking most of the proceeds. This is the question where a cross-border accountant genuinely earns their fee. See File 08.

{{/if}}{{#if section:per_vendor}}

Also worth asking

"We are co-owners — is the split on the title what we both think it is?"

Why: the withholding on a missing certificate is 15% of that owner's share, so the ownership split decides the amount. Worth confirming before settlement rather than after.

{{/if}}

frcgw-06.name: Your Pre-Settlement Plan
frcgw-06.desc: What to do, in order, between now and settlement.
frcgw-06.content:
{{#unless state:settled}}

Your pre-settlement plan

{{#if has:settlement_date}}

Settlement: {{bind:settlement_date}} · Lodge by: {{bind:lodge_by_date}} · Days to settlement: {{bind:days_to_settlement}}

{{/if}}{{#unless has:settlement_date}}

You did not give us a settlement date, so the steps below are sequenced rather than dated. Put your settlement date in your calendar first, then work backwards from it.

{{/unless}}{{/unless}}{{#if section:recovery}}

Your recovery plan

Your settlement has already happened. The 15% was remitted to the ATO and is credited to you; the sequence below is how you claim it.

{{/if}}{{#if state:have_cert}}

Closing this sale out

Your settlement has already happened and a valid certificate was provided, so nothing was withheld and nothing is outstanding. The short sequence below is record-keeping.

{{/if}}{{#unless suppress:apply_now}}

Phase 1 — Now

  1. Check the vendor name on the title and note it exactly as written.
  2. Confirm your residency for tax purposes if there is any doubt about it.
  3. Lodge the application at ato.gov.au/clearancecertificate. It is free and takes a few minutes. Supply your tax file number — it is optional, but it is what lets the application process automatically.
    4. {{#if section:per_vendor}}
  4. Make sure every owner on the title lodges their own application. One per owner, not one per property.
    5. {{/if}}

Phase 2 — Within days

  1. Most certificates issue within days. Check whether yours has.
  2. If it has issued, check the name on it against the title before you do anything else.
  3. Send it to the purchaser's conveyancer with the cover note in File 03, and ask for written confirmation of receipt.
{{/unless}}{{#if state:pending}}

Phase 1 — Now

  1. Check the status of the application you have already lodged. There is nothing further to apply for.
  2. Send the pending-notice in File 03 to the purchaser's conveyancer, so the position is known in advance rather than discovered at settlement.
    3. {{#if section:variation}}
  3. Confirm you lodged the right instrument. A clearance certificate is not available to foreign residents — see File 08.
    4. {{/if}}

Phase 2 — Until it issues

  1. Check daily as settlement approaches.
  2. The moment it issues, check the name against the title, then send it with the cover note in File 03 and get written confirmation.
{{/if}}{{#if section:recovery}}

Phase 1 — Now

You did not hold a certificate at settlement — there is nothing to apply for on this sale; File 07 is your route.

  1. Get the payment confirmation from the purchaser's conveyancer showing the amount remitted to the ATO.
  2. Confirm the contract date, which decides the income year the credit is claimed in.
    3. {{#if section:residency_first}}
  3. Settle your residency for tax purposes — it decides how much of the withheld amount comes back.
    4. {{/if}}{{#if section:variation}}
  4. Read File 08 before your next sale: a variation notice, applied for once the contract is signed, is what reduces the amount withheld.
    5. {{/if}}

Phase 2 — At the next return

  1. Make sure whoever prepares your return knows a credit is coming, so it is claimed rather than missed.
  2. Expect the timing to follow the contract year, not the settlement date — see File 07.
{{/if}}{{#if state:have_cert}}

Phase 1 — Now

You provided a valid certificate at or before settlement, so no withholding was due. There is nothing left to lodge on this sale.

  1. Keep the certificate and the written confirmation of receipt with your settlement papers.
  2. Note the issue date: the certificate is valid for 12 months and may still cover another sale in that window.
{{/if}}{{#unless state:settled}}

Phase 3 — The week before settlement

  1. Confirm in writing that the purchaser's side holds the certificate and that the name matches.
    2. {{#if section:per_vendor}}
  2. Confirm this separately for each owner. One owner's confirmation says nothing about another's.
    3. {{/if}}
  3. If a certificate has still not issued, tell the purchaser's conveyancer in writing now, so it is a known position rather than a surprise.

Phase 4 — If a certificate is not held at settlement

The purchaser withholds 15% of the sale price and remits it to the ATO. This is not a loss and it is not a penalty — the amount is credited to you, and you claim it in the return for the income year the contract was signed. File 07 sets out exactly how that works and what the timing looks like.

There is no need to try to delay settlement over this. A settlement date is a contractual obligation to the purchaser and the withholding is recoverable; the two are not comparable problems.

{{/unless}}

frcgw-07.name: Recovering A Withheld Amount
frcgw-07.desc: Where the money went, how you claim it, and how long it takes.
frcgw-07.content:
Recovering a withheld amount

Where the money is

The purchaser did not keep it, and it is not sitting in anybody's trust account. The purchaser was required to pay the withheld amount to the ATO at or before settlement, and to report the payment. It is held by the ATO as a credit in your name.

How you claim it

You claim the credit by lodging your Australian income tax return for the income year in which the contract was signed.

The contract year, not the settlement year. The capital gains event happens on the contract date. A contract signed in June 2026 and settled in August 2026 belongs to the 2025–26 income year, and the credit is claimed in that return — even though the money did not move until the following year.

How much comes back

{{#if section:variation}}

As a foreign resident, the withheld amount is credited against the capital gains tax you actually owe on the disposal. If the credit is larger than your liability, the balance is refunded. If your liability is larger, the credit reduces what remains to pay. The withholding is not a final tax.

{{/if}}{{#unless section:variation}}

If you are an Australian resident for tax purposes, have no other tax debts, and no capital gains tax is payable on the sale — a main residence held for the whole ownership period, for instance — the withheld amount is refunded in full.

If you do have capital gains tax to pay, the credit is applied against it and the balance is refunded. If you have other tax debts, the credit is applied to those first.

{{/unless}}

How long it takes

The wait is a function of where the contract date falls in the income year, not of ATO processing speed.

  • A contract signed in May settles into an income year that ends weeks later, so the return can be lodged soon after and the refund follows within weeks.
  • A contract signed in July sits at the start of an income year that does not end for another eleven months. Adding lodgement and processing, the gap between settlement and refund can reach around 15 months.

Nothing you do speeds this up materially — the return cannot be lodged before the income year ends. That asymmetry is the real argument for applying for the certificate early, and it is worth understanding rather than worrying about: the money is not at risk, it is just not available.

Worked examples

Illustrations, not your figures.

Sale priceWithheld and remitted to ATORefunded if no CGT payable and no tax debts
$450,000$67,500$67,500
$900,000$135,000$135,000
$1,200,000$180,000$180,000

What to do now

  1. Get the payment confirmation from the purchaser's conveyancer — the ATO receipt for the withheld amount. You want it on file.
  2. Confirm the contract date and therefore which income year the sale falls in.
  3. Make sure whoever prepares your return knows a credit is coming, so it is claimed rather than missed. It does not appear automatically in every case.
    4. {{#if section:residency_first}}
  4. Settle your residency for tax purposes — it decides whether the whole amount comes back or only the part above your actual liability.
    5. {{/if}}

There is no separate refund application, no early-release process, and no dispute mechanism for a correctly withheld amount. The withholding was the purchaser complying with the law, not an error to be reversed. The return is the route.

frcgw-08.name: Foreign Resident Variation Notice
frcgw-08.desc: The instrument that replaces the clearance certificate, and the trap in it.
frcgw-08.content:
Foreign resident variation notice

A clearance certificate is only issued to Australian residents for tax purposes. If you are a foreign resident, applying for one will not produce the result you want. The instrument available to you is a variation notice.

What a variation notice does

The default for a foreign resident vendor is that the purchaser withholds 15% of the sale price and remits it to the ATO. A variation notice asks the ATO to set a different rate for your sale — anywhere from 0% to 14.99%. It does not change what tax you owe; it changes how much is taken at settlement, so that the amount withheld is closer to your actual liability.

The grounds that work

A variation is granted on evidence, not on inconvenience. The grounds that are actually accepted:

  • You will not make a capital gain on the disposal. A sale at or below cost base — genuinely common where a property was bought near the top of a market.
  • Your capital gains tax liability is lower than the amount that would be withheld, including where carried-forward capital losses reduce it.
  • A mortgagee is taking so much of the proceeds that there is not enough left to fund the withholding. This is the case where the sale cannot physically complete otherwise.

"I need the cash" is not a ground. Neither is "I intend to return to Australia".

The trap: the notice states a maximum sale price

A variation notice is issued in respect of a sale up to a stated maximum price. If the property sells for more than that figure, the notice does not apply and the purchaser reverts to withholding the full 15%.

This bites at auction, and it bites where a variation was obtained early on a conservative estimate and the market moved. If your expected price changes after the notice issues, apply again with the higher figure. Do not assume a notice obtained at one price covers a sale at another.

When to apply

As soon as the contract is signed. A variation application asks for details of the actual sale, so it cannot sensibly be lodged before there is one — which makes it the opposite of the clearance certificate, where the advice is to apply before you even list.

Allow more time than a clearance certificate takes. A variation is assessed on its merits by a person, not matched automatically against a record.

{{#if section:recovery}}

Settlement has already passed in your case. A variation notice cannot be applied retrospectively — its only function is to reduce what is withheld at a settlement that has not happened yet. Your route is File 07: the amount withheld was remitted to the ATO and is credited against the capital gains tax you actually owe, claimed in the return for the income year the contract was signed.

{{/if}}

Deceased estates

A separate instrument exists for a related situation: where a property passes to beneficiaries under a will, a legislative instrument provides for nil withholding on that transfer. It is not a variation notice and it is not applied for in the same way. If you are dealing with a deceased estate rather than an ordinary sale, say so to your conveyancer early — the wrong form here wastes weeks.

Getting help

This is the part of FRCGW where professional advice is worth paying for. The grounds are evidentiary, the maximum-price mechanic catches people out, and a cross-border tax adviser will have done it before. Apply at ato.gov.au/clearancecertificate, which is also the entry point for variation applications.
